claim: The heart contains numerous interstitial cell types including fibroblast, vascular and immune cells.
source: Besides cardiomyocytes (CM), the heart contains numerous interstitial cell types which play key roles in heart repair, regeneration and disease, including fibroblast, vascular and immune cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information about cardiac cell composition.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing was performed on the total non-CM fraction and enriched (Pdgfra-GFP+) fibroblast lineage cells from murine hearts at days 3 and 7 post-sham or myocardial infarction surgery.
source: We performed single-cell RNA-sequencing of the total non-CM fraction and enriched (Pdgfra-GFP+) fibroblast lineage cells from murine hearts at days 3 and 7 post-sham or myocardial infarction (MI) surgery.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Clustering of >30,000 single cells identified >30 populations representing nine cell lineages.
source: Clustering of >30,000 single cells identified >30 populations representing nine cell lineages, including a previously undescribed fibroblast lineage trajectory present in both sham and MI hearts leading to a uniquely activated cell state defined in part by a strong anti-WNT transcriptome signature.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the clustering analysis of the scRNA-seq data.

claim: A previously undescribed fibroblast lineage trajectory was identified that is present in both sham and MI hearts.
source: Clustering of >30,000 single cells identified >30 populations representing nine cell lineages, including a previously undescribed fibroblast lineage trajectory present in both sham and MI hearts leading to a uniquely activated cell state defined in part by a strong anti-WNT transcriptome signature.
evidence: This is a novel finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The previously undescribed fibroblast lineage trajectory leads to a uniquely activated cell state defined in part by a strong anti-WNT transcriptome signature.
source: Clustering of >30,000 single cells identified >30 populations representing nine cell lineages, including a previously undescribed fibroblast lineage trajectory present in both sham and MI hearts leading to a uniquely activated cell state defined in part by a strong anti-WNT transcriptome signature.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the novel fibroblast population identified.

claim: Novel myofibroblast subtypes expressing either pro-fibrotic or anti-fibrotic signatures were uncovered.
source: We also uncovered novel myofibroblast subtypes expressing either pro-fibrotic or anti-fibrotic signatures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study reported in the abstract.

claim: The data highlight non-linear dynamics in myeloid and fibroblast lineages after cardiac injury.
source: Our data highlight non-linear dynamics in myeloid and fibroblast lineages after cardiac injury, and provide an entry point for deeper analysis of cardiac homeostasis, inflammation, fibrosis, repair and regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trajectory analysis of the data.

claim: Cardiovascular disease including myocardial infarction remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the Western and developing worlds.
source: Cardiovascular disease including myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the Western and developing worlds.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge cited as background.

claim: After acute MI, millions of cardiomyocytes are lost by necrosis and apoptosis.
source: After acute MI, millions of cardiomyocytes (CM) are lost by necrosis and apoptosis, and an initially adaptive collagen-rich scar is laid down to preserve chamber geometry and prevent rupture.
evidence: This describes the pathophysiology of MI based on established knowledge.

claim: An initially adaptive collagen-rich scar is laid down after MI to preserve chamber geometry and prevent rupture.
source: After acute MI, millions of cardiomyocytes (CM) are lost by necrosis and apoptosis, and an initially adaptive collagen-rich scar is laid down to preserve chamber geometry and prevent rupture.
evidence: This describes the physiological response to MI based on established knowledge.

claim: The mammalian heart is regarded as being poorly regenerative.
source: The mammalian heart is regarded as being poorly regenerative as the long-term sequelae in virtually all etiologies of heart disease involve increased wall stiffness, reduced heart function and progression to heart failure.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cardiac biology.

claim: Some inbred strains of mice show surprising cardiac reparative abilities.
source: However, some inbred strains of mice show surprising cardiac reparative abilities (Patterson et al., 2017), and CM renewal and heart regeneration can be stimulated experimentally (D'Uva et al., 2015; Mohamed et al., 2018; Srivastava and DeWitt, 2016; Wang et al., 2018), garnering optimism that heart regeneration can be achieved in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Patterson et al., 2017.

claim: CM renewal and heart regeneration can be stimulated experimentally.
source: However, some inbred strains of mice show surprising cardiac reparative abilities (Patterson et al., 2017), and CM renewal and heart regeneration can be stimulated experimentally (D'Uva et al., 2015; Mohamed et al., 2018; Srivastava and DeWitt, 2016; Wang et al., 2018), garnering optimism that heart regeneration can be achieved in humans.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Cardiac fibroblasts represent ~10% of all cardiac cells.
source: Cardiac fibroblasts represent ~10% of all cardiac cells (Pinto et al., 2016) and are distributed throughout the cardiac interstitial, perivascular and sub-epicardial spaces, where they are proposed to have sentinel, paracrine, mechanical, extracellular matrix (ECM) and electrical functions (Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014; Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pinto et al., 2016.

claim: Cardiac fibroblasts are distributed throughout the cardiac interstitial, perivascular and sub-epicardial spaces.
source: Cardiac fibroblasts represent ~10% of all cardiac cells (Pinto et al., 2016) and are distributed throughout the cardiac interstitial, perivascular and sub-epicardial spaces, where they are proposed to have sentinel, paracrine, mechanical, extracellular matrix (ECM) and electrical functions (Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014; Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017).
evidence: This describes the anatomical distribution of cardiac fibroblasts based on cited literature.

claim: Cardiac fibroblasts are proposed to have sentinel, paracrine, mechanical, extracellular matrix (ECM) and electrical functions.
source: Cardiac fibroblasts represent ~10% of all cardiac cells (Pinto et al., 2016) and are distributed throughout the cardiac interstitial, perivascular and sub-epicardial spaces, where they are proposed to have sentinel, paracrine, mechanical, extracellular matrix (ECM) and electrical functions (Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014; Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014 and Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017.

claim: After injury, inflammation is principally executed by poly-functional monocytes and macrophages.
source: After injury, inflammation is principally executed by poly-functional monocytes (Mo) and macrophages (MΦ), and is necessary to protect against pathogens and autoimmunity, and to coordinate healing.
evidence: This describes the role of immune cells in cardiac injury based on established knowledge.

claim: Fibroblasts participate in inflammation and phagocytosis and are the principal drivers of fibrotic repair.
source: Fibroblasts also participate in inflammation and phagocytosis and are the principal drivers of fibrotic repair (Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014; Gourdie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shinde and Frangogiannis, 2014 and Gourdie et al., 2016.

claim: Timely resolution of inflammation is necessary for limiting fibrosis and enabling tissue replacement in heart repair.
source: In heart repair, timely resolution of inflammation is necessary for limiting fibrosis and enabling tissue replacement, while uncontrolled inflammation leads to increased fibrosis and chamber wall stiffening, poor electro-mechanical coupling, continued loss of CMs and worsening outcomes (Mescher, 2017; Lai et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Uncontrolled inflammation leads to increased fibrosis and chamber wall stiffening, poor electro-mechanical coupling, continued loss of CMs and worsening outcomes.
source: In heart repair, timely resolution of inflammation is necessary for limiting fibrosis and enabling tissue replacement, while uncontrolled inflammation leads to increased fibrosis and chamber wall stiffening, poor electro-mechanical coupling, continued loss of CMs and worsening outcomes (Mescher, 2017; Lai et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mescher, 2017; Lai et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2018.

claim: Transcriptional profiles of 13,331 cells were captured after quality control filtering from TIP.
source: Transcriptional profiles of 13,331 cells were captured after quality control filtering (sham: 5,723; MI-day 3: 3,875; MI-day 7: 3,733).
evidence: This describes the number of cells analyzed in the TIP dataset.

claim: TIP cells were represented by a total of 24 populations and nine distinct cell lineages.
source: TIP cells were represented by a total of 24 populations and nine distinct cell lineages (Figure 1A–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the clustering analysis, supported by Figure 1.

claim: Major cell types in TIP comprised fibroblasts/myofibroblasts (Col1a1+Pdgfra+GFP+), endothelial cells (Kdr+Pecam1+), mural cells (Cspg4+Pdgfrb+), Mo and MΦ (Cd68+Itgam+), dendritic-like cells (Cd209a+Itgam+), glial cells (Plp1+Kcna1+), B-cells (Cd79a+Ms4a1+), T-cells (Cd3e+Cd3d+Lef1+) and natural killer cells (Klrk1+Ccl5+).
source: Major cell types comprised fibroblasts/myofibroblasts (Col1a1+Pdgfra+GFP+), endothelial cells (ECs; Kdr+Pecam1+), mural cells (Cspg4+Pdgfrb+), Mo and MΦ (Cd68+Itgam+), dendritic-like (DC) cells (Cd209a+Itgam+), glial cells (Plp1+Kcna1+), B-cells (Cd79a+Ms4a1+), T-cells (Cd3e+Cd3d+Lef1+) and natural killer cells (NKCs; Klrk1+Ccl5+) (Figure 1A–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the major cell types identified with their marker genes, supported by Figure 1.

claim: Vtn, encoding Vitronectin, was specifically expressed in mural cells.
source: New lineage markers were identified; for example, Vtn, encoding Vitronectin, was specifically expressed in mural cells, whereas Kcna1, encoding the potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily A member 1, was highly specific to glial cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a novel marker identified in the study, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Kcna1, encoding the potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily A member 1, was highly specific to glial cells.
source: New lineage markers were identified; for example, Vtn, encoding Vitronectin, was specifically expressed in mural cells, whereas Kcna1, encoding the potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily A member 1, was highly specific to glial cells (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a novel marker identified in the study, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: There were three major sub-populations of ECs (EC1, EC2, EC3), comprising vascular and lymphatic lineages.
source: There were three major sub-populations of ECs (EC1, EC2, EC3), comprising vascular and lymphatic lineages (Pecam1+Kdr+Ly6a+) (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes the EC sub-populations identified, supported by Figure 1.

claim: The majority EC1 population expressed Ly6a (encoding SCA1) as well as the vascular transcription factor Sox17, and likely represents microvascular ECs.
source: The majority EC1 population expressed Ly6a (encoding SCA1) as well as the vascular transcription factor (TF) Sox17, and likely represents microvascular ECs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression data for EC1.

claim: EC2 expressed canonical arterial endothelial markers such as Bmx, Sema3g and Efnb2, as well as TF genes Sox17 and Hey1.
source: EC2 expressed canonical arterial endothelial markers such as Bmx, Sema3g and Efnb2, as well as TF genes Sox17 and Hey1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), the latter acting downstream of NOTCH which is required for arterial EC fate.
evidence: This describes the marker genes for EC2, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Hey1 acts downstream of NOTCH which is required for arterial EC fate.
source: EC2 expressed canonical arterial endothelial markers such as Bmx, Sema3g and Efnb2, as well as TF genes Sox17 and Hey1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), the latter acting downstream of NOTCH which is required for arterial EC fate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the NOTCH pathway in arterial EC specification.

claim: EC3 almost uniquely expressed venous EC marker Nr2f2 (encoding COUPTFII) and Von Willebrand factor (Vwf).
source: EC3 almost uniquely expressed venous EC marker Nr2f2 (encoding COUPTFII) and Von Willebrand factor (Vwf), and a minority (~3%) expressed Prox1 and Lyve1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), consistent with a lymphatic identity.
evidence: This describes the marker genes for EC3, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A minority (~3%) of EC3 expressed Prox1 and Lyve1, consistent with a lymphatic identity.
source: EC3 almost uniquely expressed venous EC marker Nr2f2 (encoding COUPTFII) and Von Willebrand factor (Vwf), and a minority (~3%) expressed Prox1 and Lyve1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), consistent with a lymphatic identity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression data for a subset of EC3.

claim: The EC data are broadly consistent with recently published single-cell data.
source: Our EC data are broadly consistent with recently published single-cell data (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares the current findings to a previous study by Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: A single B-cell population (BC) expressed Cd79a, Ms4a1 and Ly6d.
source: Among lymphocytes, a single B-cell population (BC) expressed Cd79a, Ms4a1 and Ly6d (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This describes the marker genes for the B-cell population, supported by Figure 1.

claim: T-cell sub-populations TC1-Cd8 (Cd8a+) and TC2-Cd4 (Cd4+Lef1+) likely represent cytotoxic and helper T-cells, respectively.
source: T-cell sub-populations TC1-Cd8 (Cd8a+) and TC2-Cd4 (Cd4+Lef1+) likely represent cytotoxic and helper T-cells, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the T-cell sub-populations based on marker gene expression.

claim: NKCs exclusively expressed Klrk1 and upregulated Lck, Ccl5 and Ctsw.
source: NKCs exclusively expressed Klrk1 and upregulated Lck, Ccl5 and Ctsw (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This describes the marker genes for NKCs, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Major injury-induced cellular responses and flux were observed after MI, including expansion of Mo/MΦ populations at MI-day 3, as well as myofibroblasts and an additional MΦ population at MI-day 7.
source: We observed major injury-induced cellular responses and flux after MI, including expansion of Mo/MΦ populations at MI-day 3, as well as myofibroblasts and an additional MΦ population at MI-day 7 (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of cell populations after MI, supported by Figure 1.

claim: DPA identified 12 populations showing significant (p<0.01) flux between conditions.
source: DPA identified 12 populations showing significant (p<0.01) flux between conditions (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 2); for example, the fibroblast sub-populations F-SL and F-SH (see below) decreased sharply in proportion at MI-day 3, while M1 and M2 MΦ populations expanded at days 3 and 7 after MI, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the differential proportion analysis, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: The fibroblast sub-populations F-SL and F-SH decreased sharply in proportion at MI-day 3.
source: DPA identified 12 populations showing significant (p<0.01) flux between conditions (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 2); for example, the fibroblast sub-populations F-SL and F-SH (see below) decreased sharply in proportion at MI-day 3, while M1 and M2 MΦ populations expanded at days 3 and 7 after MI, respectively.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the DPA analysis, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: M1 and M2 MΦ populations expanded at days 3 and 7 after MI, respectively.
source: DPA identified 12 populations showing significant (p<0.01) flux between conditions (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 2); for example, the fibroblast sub-populations F-SL and F-SH (see below) decreased sharply in proportion at MI-day 3, while M1 and M2 MΦ populations expanded at days 3 and 7 after MI, respectively.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the DPA analysis, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: Cardiac tissue-resident MΦ originate from CX3CR1+ progenitors in the yolk sac and Mo from fetal liver and post-natal bone marrow.
source: Cardiac tissue-resident MΦ originate from CX3CR1+ progenitors in the yolk sac and Mo from fetal liver and post-natal bone marrow (Ensan et al., 2016), and have roles in immunity, coronary artery and pacemaker development, and heart regeneration (Lavine et al., 2014; Hulsmans et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ensan et al., 2016.

claim: Cardiac tissue-resident MΦ have roles in immunity, coronary artery and pacemaker development, and heart regeneration.
source: Cardiac tissue-resident MΦ originate from CX3CR1+ progenitors in the yolk sac and Mo from fetal liver and post-natal bone marrow (Ensan et al., 2016), and have roles in immunity, coronary artery and pacemaker development, and heart regeneration (Lavine et al., 2014; Hulsmans et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lavine et al., 2014 and Hulsmans et al., 2017.

claim: Resident MΦ are long lived and self-renewing.
source: Resident MΦ are long lived and self-renewing (Epelman et al., 2014; Bajpai et al., 2018), although some are supplanted by blood-derived Mo with age or injury (Heidt et al., 2014; Molawi et al., 2014; Dick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Epelman et al., 2014 and Bajpai et al., 2018.

claim: Some resident MΦ are supplanted by blood-derived Mo with age or injury.
source: Resident MΦ are long lived and self-renewing (Epelman et al., 2014; Bajpai et al., 2018), although some are supplanted by blood-derived Mo with age or injury (Heidt et al., 2014; Molawi et al., 2014; Dick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heidt et al., 2014; Molawi et al., 2014; Dick et al., 2019.

claim: MI triggers a biphasic cascade of inflammation and remodeling, with the acute phase involving early influx of neutrophils and CCR2+LY6C2high pro-inflammatory M1 Mo/MΦ.
source: MI triggers a biphasic cascade of inflammation and remodeling, with the acute phase involving early influx of neutrophils and CCR2+LY6C2high pro-inflammatory M1 Mo/MΦ, which phagocytose debris and secrete pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6 and TNFα to amplify the inflammatory response (Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018.

claim: M1 Mo/MΦ phagocytose debris and secrete pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6 and TNFα to amplify the inflammatory response.
source: MI triggers a biphasic cascade of inflammation and remodeling, with the acute phase involving early influx of neutrophils and CCR2+LY6C2high pro-inflammatory M1 Mo/MΦ, which phagocytose debris and secrete pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6 and TNFα to amplify the inflammatory response (Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018.

claim: The repair phase begins around MI-day 3 when non-classical LY6C2-F4/80high M2 MΦ accumulate and secrete anti-inflammatory cytokines such as Il-10 and TGF-β, and stimulate angiogenesis.
source: The repair phase begins around MI-day 3 when non-classical LY6C2-F4/80high M2 MΦ accumulate and secrete anti-inflammatory cytokines such as Il-10 and TGF-β, and stimulate angiogenesis (Epelman et al., 2015; Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Epelman et al., 2015 and Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018.

claim: In sham hearts, cardiac tissue-resident MΦ were identified with the signature Cx3cr1highAdgre1(F4/80)highH2-Aa(MHC-II)+Itgam(CD11b)lowLy6c2lowCcr2- (MAC-TR).
source: In sham hearts, we identified cardiac tissue-resident MΦ with the signature Cx3cr1highAdgre1(F4/80)highH2-Aa(MHC-II)+Itgam(CD11b)lowLy6c2lowCcr2- (MAC-TR; Figure 1A,B; Figure 2A–D) (Ensan et al., 2016; Epelman et al., 2014; Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018; Lavine et al., 2014; Lavine et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the marker signature for tissue-resident MΦ, supported by Figure 2 and multiple citations.

claim: A pro-regenerative population with the signature TIMD4+LYVE1+MHC-IIlowCCR2- self-renews and is not replaced by blood monocytes even after injury.
source: Recent work using flow cytometry and scRNA-seq has delineated several subsets of cardiac tissue-resident MΦ, including a pro-regenerative population with the signature TIMD4+LYVE1+MHC-IIlowCCR2-, that self-renew and are not replaced by blood monocytes even after injury (Dick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dick et al., 2019.

claim: The TIMD4+LYVE1+MHC-IIlowCCR2- population could be discerned at the scRNA-seq level as a subset within MAC-TR, which persisted after injury.
source: We could discern this same population at the scRNA-seq level as a subset within MAC-TR, which persisted after injury (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by Figure 2.

claim: The additional major subset of CCR2- tissue-resident MΦ has a low monocyte dependence during homeostasis but is almost fully replaced by monocytes after MI.
source: The additional major subset of CCR2- tissue-resident MΦ (Dick et al., 2019) could also be recognised at the scRNA-seq level as the Timd4-Lyve1-H2-Aa(MHC-II)highCcr2- subset of MAC-TR – this population has been shown to have a low monocyte dependence during homeostasis but is almost fully replaced by monocytes after MI (Dick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dick et al., 2019.

claim: At MI-day 3, a major influx population was identified as classical blood-derived M1 Mo, based on the signature Adgre1(F4/80)+Itgam(CD11b)+Fcgr1(CD64)+Ly6c2highCcr2highH2-Aa(MHC-II)low (M1Mo).
source: At MI-day 3, a major influx population was identified as classical blood-derived M1 Mo, based on the signature Adgre1(F4/80)+Itgam(CD11b)+Fcgr1(CD64)+Ly6c2highCcr2highH2-Aa(MHC-II)low (M1Mo; Figure 2A–C) (Epelman et al., 2015; Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018).
evidence: This describes the marker signature for M1 Mo, supported by Figure 2 and citations.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in M1Mo showed Gene Ontology (GO) term over-representation for cell migration, inflammation and T cell activation.
source: Differentially expressed genes showed Gene Ontology (GO) term over-representation for cell migration, inflammation and T cell activation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of M1Mo, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: The more abundant population at MI-day 3 was identified as classical Mo-derived M1 MΦ based on the signature Ccr2highAdgre1(F4/80)+Ly6c2+H2-Aa(MHC-II)+ (M1MΦ).
source: The more abundant population at MI-day 3 was identified as classical Mo-derived M1 MΦ based on the signature Ccr2highAdgre1(F4/80)+Ly6c2+H2-Aa(MHC-II)+ (M1MΦ; Figure 1A,B; Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This describes the marker signature for M1 MΦ, supported by Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Hierarchical clustering showed M1MΦ to be most closely related to M1Mo.
source: This assignment was supported by expression of the additional MΦ markers cited above, including Mertk and C1q, and hierarchical clustering, which showed M1MΦ to be most closely related to M1Mo (Figure 1C), as for human cognates (Bajpai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a result from hierarchical clustering analysis, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in M1MΦ showed GO term over-representation for leukocyte migration and responses to interleukin-1.
source: Differentially expressed genes showed GO term over-representation for leukocyte migration and responses to interleukin-1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of M1MΦ, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: The most prominent population at MI-day 7 was identified as non-classical M2 MΦ involved in inflammation resolution and repair, with the signature Ccr2highAdgre1(F4/80)+H2-Aa(MHC-II)highLy6c2- (M2MΦ).
source: The most prominent population at MI-day 7 was identified as non-classical M2 MΦ involved in inflammation resolution and repair, with the signature Ccr2highAdgre1(F4/80)+H2-Aa(MHC-II)highLy6c2- (M2MΦ; Figure 1A,B; Figure 2A–D) (Epelman et al., 2015; Swirski and Nahrendorf, 2018).
evidence: This describes the marker signature for M2 MΦ, supported by Figures 1 and 2 and citations.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in M2MΦ showed GO term over-representation for antigen presentation via MHC class II.
source: Differentially expressed genes showed GO term over-representation for antigen presentation via MHC class II (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of M2MΦ, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: The non-classical M2 MΦ population increased late during injury repair from <2% of TIP in sham and MI-day 3 hearts, to 16% at MI-day 7.
source: As expected, the non-classical M2 MΦ population increased late during injury repair from <2% of TIP in sham and MI-day 3 hearts, to 16% at MI-day 7.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of M2 MΦ expansion.

claim: The population dendrogram showed that M2MΦ were most closely related to MAC-TR.
source: Interestingly, the population dendrogram showed that M2MΦ were most closely related to MAC-TR (Figure 1C), and similarities between resident and subsets of infiltrating Mo/MΦ have been discerned recently using single-cell methods (Dick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from hierarchical clustering analysis, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Both MAC-TR and M2MΦ expressed Cx3cr1, often used to define tissue-resident MΦ.
source: Both MAC-TR and M2MΦ expressed Cx3cr1, often used to define tissue-resident MΦ (Figure 2B), and both upregulated pro-regenerative genes Igf1 (Figure 2B) and Pdgfb/c (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes shared marker expression between MAC-TR and M2MΦ, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Both MAC-TR and M2MΦ upregulated pro-regenerative genes Igf1 and Pdgfb/c.
source: Both MAC-TR and M2MΦ expressed Cx3cr1, often used to define tissue-resident MΦ (Figure 2B), and both upregulated pro-regenerative genes Igf1 (Figure 2B) and Pdgfb/c (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes shared gene expression between MAC-TR and M2MΦ, supported by Figure 2.

claim: The majority of M2MΦ were Ccr2high; however, a minor sub-population was Ccr2low and these expressed the highest levels of Igf1 and lower levels of MHC-II.
source: The majority of M2MΦ were Ccr2high (important for migration); however, a minor sub-populaion was Ccr2low (arrows, Figure 2B) and these expressed the highest levels of Igf1 and lower levels of MHC-II (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes heterogeneity within the M2MΦ population, supported by Figure 2.

claim: Diffusion Map analysis applied to major Mo/MΦ populations revealed a continuum of states resolved into a trajectory from early infiltrating M1Mo and inflammatory M1MΦ, to the late peaking M2MΦ.
source: Diffusion Map (Angerer et al., 2016) analysis applied to model possible temporal (pseudotime) changes in major Mo/MΦ populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) revealed a continuum of states resolved into a trajectory from early infiltrating M1Mo (left) and inflammatory M1MΦ (centre), to the late peaking M2MΦ (right), similar to a recent scRNA-seq study (Dick et al., 2019) and consistent with the current model in which M1 Mo differentiate into M2 cells in situ (Lavine et al., 2018; Hilgendorf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map trajectory analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citations.

claim: The Diffusion Map demonstrated the convergence of M2MΦ present at MI-day 7 with tissue-resident MΦ (MAC-TR) in sham hearts.
source: The Diffusion Map also demonstrated the convergence of M2MΦ present at MI-day 7 with tissue-resident MΦ (MAC-TR) in sham hearts, a relationship reflected in the population dendrogram (Figure 1C; see Discussion).
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map analysis, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: MAC-IFNIC cells showed strong upregulation of interferon (IFN)-induced genes including Ifit3, Ifit1 and Cxcl10.
source: MAC-IFNIC cells showed strong upregulation of interferon (IFN)-induced genes including Ifit3, Ifit1 and Cxcl10 (Figure 2C), consistent with GO term analysis implicating responses to IFN α, β, and γ (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the gene expression signature of MAC-IFNIC cells, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: MAC-IFNIC cells appear to arise from Ccr2+ MΦ as opposed to monocytes.
source: These cells appear to arise from Ccr2+ MΦ as opposed to monocytes (Dick et al., 2019), and likely correspond to the recently described inflammatory MΦ subtype that has negative effects on heart repair after MI through promotion of inflammatory cell types, and cytokine and chemokine expression (King et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dick et al., 2019 and King et al., 2017.

claim: 91 cell-cell relationships with weighted paths higher than expected by chance (Padj <0.01) were identified in the cell-cell communication network.
source: Based on permutation testing of randomized network connections, 91 cell-cell relationships with weighted paths higher than expected by chance (Padj <0.01) were identified (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a result from the cell-cell communication network analysis, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Myofibroblasts (MYO) and MΦ populations M1MΦ and MAC-8 exhibited the largest number of outbound connections, with MYO having the highest weight.
source: Myofibroblasts (MYO) and MΦ populations M1MΦ and MAC-8 exhibited the largest number of outbound connections, with MYO having the highest weight.
evidence: This is a result from the cell-cell communication network analysis.

claim: ECs by far showed the largest number and weighting of significant inbound connections.
source: ECs by far showed the largest number and weighting of significant inbound connections.
evidence: This is a result from the cell-cell communication network analysis.

claim: Fibroblast populations (F-SH, F-SL, F-Act and F-WntX) appeared to communicate exclusively with vascular (ECs and mural) and glial cells.
source: Strikingly, fibroblast populations (F-SH, F-SL, F-Act and F-WntX) appeared to communicate exclusively with vascular (ECs and mural) and glial cells.
evidence: This is a result from the cell-cell communication network analysis.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of sham and MI-day 3 hearts showed that Pdgfra-GFP+ fibroblasts were observed in close spatial relationships or direct contact with CD31+ endothelial cells.
source: In line with this result, immunofluorescence analysis of sham and MI-day 3 hearts showed that Pdgfra-GFP+ fibroblasts were observed in close spatial relationships or direct contact with CD31+ endothelial cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a result from immunofluorescence imaging, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Top-weighted interactions involving MYO were driven mostly by ECM-associated ligands including COL1a1, COL1a2, Fibronectin 1, Pleiotrophin, COL3a1, COL5a2, Biglycan, Metalloprotease inhibitor one and COL5a1.
source: Top-weighted interactions involving MYO were driven mostly by ECM-associated ligands including COL1a1, COL1a2, Fibronectin 1, Pleiotrophin, COL3a1, COL5a2, Biglycan, Metalloprotease inhibitor one and COL5a1, that can engage with receptors expressed in numerous populations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the ligand-receptor network analysis, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Glial cells expressed canonical neuronal glia markers, including Plp1, Prnp and Gfra3.
source: The minority glial cell population expressed canonical neuronal glia markers, including Plp1, Prnp and Gfra3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and likely support cardiac sympathetic nerves essential for cardiac regeneration in neonates (Mahmoud et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the marker genes for glial cells, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Glial cells likely support cardiac sympathetic nerves essential for cardiac regeneration in neonates.
source: The minority glial cell population expressed canonical neuronal glia markers, including Plp1, Prnp and Gfra3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and likely support cardiac sympathetic nerves essential for cardiac regeneration in neonates (Mahmoud et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression and citation to Mahmoud et al., 2015.

claim: Glial cells appeared to communicate with the three EC populations and mural cells.
source: Glial cells also appeared to communicate with the three EC populations and mural cells (Figure 3A), consistent with the phenomenon of neurovascular congruence in the cardiac sympathetic plexus (Stubbs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from the cell-cell communication network analysis, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Eight ligands highly specific to glial cells were detected including Dhh (Desert Hedgehog) and Semaphorin genes Sema3b and Sema4f.
source: In support of this, we detected eight ligands highly specific to glial cells (expressed in <5% of other TIP cells) including Dhh (Desert Hedgehog) and Semaphorin genes Sema3b and Sema4f (Figure 3D), involved in both neural and angiogenic development (Gamboa et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes specific ligands expressed by glial cells, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Dhh, Sema3b and Sema4f are involved in both neural and angiogenic development.
source: In support of this, we detected eight ligands highly specific to glial cells (expressed in <5% of other TIP cells) including Dhh (Desert Hedgehog) and Semaphorin genes Sema3b and Sema4f (Figure 3D), involved in both neural and angiogenic development (Gamboa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gamboa et al., 2017.

claim: Five minor populations expressing markers of two lineages were detected (F-EC, M2MΦ-EC, EC-L1, EC-L2 and BC-TC).
source: We detected five minor populations expressing markers of two lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This describes hybrid populations identified in the data, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The F-EC hybrid population co-expressed markers of fibroblasts and ECs, and segregated with other fibroblast populations.
source: The F-EC hybrid population co-expressed markers of fibroblasts and ECs, and segregated with other fibroblast populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the F-EC population, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: 2.4 ± 0.28% of GFP+CD31+ cells were detected in sham hearts, 1.51 ± 0.26% in MI-day 7 hearts, and none in controls by flow cytometry.
source: We detected 2.4 ± 0.28% of GFP+CD31+ cells in sham hearts, 1.51 ± 0.26% in MI-day 7 hearts, and none in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–E) - thus, while double positive cells were found, they did not appear responsive to injury.
evidence: This is a result from flow cytometry analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: GFP+CD31+ double positive cells did not appear responsive to injury.
source: We detected 2.4 ± 0.28% of GFP+CD31+ cells in sham hearts, 1.51 ± 0.26% in MI-day 7 hearts, and none in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–E) - thus, while double positive cells were found, they did not appear responsive to injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the flow cytometry data showing no significant change with injury.

claim: The M2MΦ-EC hybrid population co-expressed markers of ECs (Kdr+Pecam1+Sox17+ Efnb+Mcam+) and M2MΦ (Ccr2highAdgre1[F4/80]+H2-Aa[MHC-II]highCx3cr1+Mrc1[CD206]+Ly6 c2-), and segregated with M2MΦ.
source: The M2MΦ-EC hybrid population co-expressed markers of ECs (Kdr+Pecam1+Sox17+ Efnb+Mcam+) and M2MΦ (Ccr2highAdgre1[F4/80]+H2-Aa[MHC-II]highCx3cr1+Mrc1[CD206]+Ly6 c2-), and segregated with M2MΦ (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the M2MΦ-EC population, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Flow cytometry revealed 0.56 ± 0.02% single live CD31+CD45+ cells in sham-day 7 hearts, increasing to 4.04 ± 1.03% in MI-day 7 hearts.
source: Flow revealed 0.56 ± 0.02% single live CD31+CD45+ cells in sham-day 7 hearts, increasing to 4.04 ± 1.03% in MI-day 7 hearts, demonstrating an increase in injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A–C).
evidence: This is a result from flow cytometry analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Among CD31+CD45+ cells, 35.67 ± 3.01% were F4/80+CD206+ in sham hearts, increasing to 60.03 ± 4.60% in MI-day 7 hearts.
source: Among these, 35.67 ± 3.01% were F4/80+CD206+ (a signature of M1 and M2 MΦ) in sham hearts, increasing to 60.03 ± 4.60% in MI-day 7 hearts.
evidence: This is a result from flow cytometry analysis of CD31+CD45+ cells.

claim: A major subset of fibroblasts in the uninjured adult murine heart express the cell surface stem/progenitor cell markers SCA1 and/or PDGFRα.
source: A major subset of fibroblasts in the uninjured adult murine heart express the cell surface stem/progenitor cell markers SCA1 and/or PDGFRα (Kanisicak et al., 2016; Asli et al., 2017; Chong et al., 2011; Noseda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: When fibroblasts differentiate into MYO, they reduce SCA1 and PDGFRα markers and express fibrogenic (e.g. Periostin; POSTN) and/or contractile (e.g. αSmooth Muscle Actin; αSMA) proteins.
source: However, when fibroblasts differentiate into MYO, they reduce these markers and express fibrogenic (e.g. Periostin; POSTN) and/or contractile (e.g. αSmooth Muscle Actin; αSMA) proteins (Fu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2018.

claim: GFP fluorescence from PdgfraGFP/+ mice was used as a surrogate lineage tracing tool and enabled capture of both GFPhigh fibroblasts as well as their derivatives in MI mice, including MYO.
source: GFP fluorescence from PdgfraGFP/+ mice was used as a surrogate lineage tracing tool and enabled us to capture both GFPhigh fibroblasts as well as their derivatives in MI mice, including MYO (Asli et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach, supported by citation to Asli et al., 2017.

claim: Unbiased clustering on an aggregate of 16,787 GFP+ cells identified 11 sub-populations.
source: We performed unbiased clustering on an aggregate of the 16,787 cells (Materials and methods), identifying 11 sub-populations (Figure 4A–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is a primary result from the clustering analysis of GFP+ cells, supported by Figure 4.

claim: All GFP+ populations showed expression of canonical fibroblast markers Pdgfra, GFP, Ddr2 and Col1a1, albeit at varying proportions and levels.
source: All populations showed expression of canonical fibroblast markers Pdgfra, GFP, Ddr2 and Col1a1, albeit at varying proportions and levels (Figure 4E), and major changes in cell proportions were seen between conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This describes the marker expression across GFP+ populations, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Two major fibroblast populations in sham conditions were distinguished and termed Fibroblast-Sca1-high (F-SH) and Fibroblast-Sca1-low (F-SL).
source: In sham conditions, two major fibroblast populations could be distinguished on the basis of scRNA-seq. We termed these Fibroblast-Sca1-high (F-SH) and Fibroblast-Sca1-low (F-SL), as the highest upregulated gene in F-SH was Ly6a(Sca1) (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the two major fibroblast populations identified, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Approximately 60% of single S+P+ cells analyzed by Fluidigm were predicted to correspond to the F-SH population.
source: Approximately 60% of single S+P+ cells analyzed by Fluidigm were predicted to correspond to the F-SH population (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), compared to <30% among total sham GFP+ cells (Figure 4D), indicating that S+P+ cells are significantly over-represented in F-SH cells (Fisher's exact test, p=8.13e-11).
evidence: This is a result from the iRF classifier prediction, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: S+P+ cells are significantly over-represented in F-SH cells (Fisher's exact test, p=8.13e-11).
source: Approximately 60% of single S+P+ cells analyzed by Fluidigm were predicted to correspond to the F-SH population (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), compared to <30% among total sham GFP+ cells (Figure 4D), indicating that S+P+ cells are significantly over-represented in F-SH cells (Fisher's exact test, p=8.13e-11).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing S+P+ cell distribution.

claim: THY1/CD90 is a recognised MSC marker, and Thy1 was upregulated in F-SH with high significance (p=4.48e-176).
source: THY1/CD90 is a recognised MSC marker, and Thy1 was upregulated in F-SH with high significance (p=4.48e-176; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This describes Thy1 expression in F-SH, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: FACS-isolated S+Pdgfra-GFP+CD90.2high cells isolated from healthy hearts showed a ~ 6 fold enrichment in cCFU-F compared to S+Pdgfra-GFP+CD90.2low cells.
source: Furthermore, FACS-isolated S+Pdgfra-GFP+CD90.2high cells isolated from healthy hearts showed a ~ 6 fold enrichment in cCFU-F compared to S+Pdgfra-GFP+CD90.2low cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is a result from the colony formation assay, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The F-SH population contains a subset of cells expressing Pdgfra, Ly6a(Sca1) and Thy1(Cd90) that is enriched in cCFU-F.
source: Together, these results show that the F-SH population contains a subset of cells expressing Pdgfra, Ly6a(Sca1) and Thy1(Cd90) that is enriched in cCFU-F, highlighting the distinct expression signatures and functional properties of F-SH and F-SL.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including marker expression and functional assays.

claim: F-SH was characterized by over-representation of genes involved in the biological process cell adhesion, which included cell surface receptor genes Ackr3(Cxcr-7), Thy1(Cd90), Axl and Cd34.
source: F-SH was characterized by over-representation of genes involved in the biological process (BP) cell adhesion, which included cell surface receptor genes Ackr3(Cxcr-7), Thy1(Cd90), Axl and Cd34.
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of differentially expressed genes in F-SH.

claim: F-SL was characterized by GO BP terms signaling and signal transduction.
source: In contrast, F-SL was characterized by GO BP terms signaling and signal transduction (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of differentially expressed genes in F-SL.

claim: Within the signal transduction category in F-SL, protein localization prediction indicated an over-represented majority (19/28) of secreted proteins (Fisher's exact test, p=0.03), with 10/19 identified as ligands.
source: Within the signal transduction category, protein localization prediction with LocTree3 (Goldberg et al., 2014) indicated an over-represented majority (19/28) of secreted proteins (Fisher's exact test, p=0.03), with 10/19 identified as ligands, including APOE, BMP4 and ADM.
evidence: This is a result from protein localization prediction and statistical analysis.

claim: F-SL has a unique secretory phenotype distinct from that in F-SH.
source: Thus, F-SL, a major sub-division of fibroblasts, has a unique secretory phenotype distinct from that in F-SH, which is enriched in MSC-like colony forming cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GO analysis and functional characterization.

claim: Two previously unstudied GFP+ fibroblast populations termed Fibroblast - Wnt expressing (F-WntX) and Fibroblast - transitory (F-Trans) were identified.
source: We identified two previously unstudied GFP+ fibroblast populations termed Fibroblast - Wnt expressing (F-WntX) and Fibroblast - transitory (F-Trans).
evidence: This describes novel populations identified in the study.

claim: F-WntX and F-Trans were present in both sham and MI hearts, although had diminished significantly by MI-day 7 (DPA; p<0.01).
source: These were present in both sham and MI hearts, although had diminished significantly by MI-day 7 (DPA; p<0.01; Figure 4D).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of F-WntX and F-Trans, supported by Figure 4D.

claim: In F-WntX, the top upregulated gene was Wif1, encoding a secreted canonical WNT pathway inhibitor essential for cardiac repair after MI.
source: In F-WntX, differential gene expression analysis showed that the top upregulated gene was Wif1, encoding a secreted canonical WNT pathway inhibitor essential for cardiac repair after MI (Meyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the top marker gene for F-WntX, supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2017.

claim: WIF1 can antagonize Connective Tissue Growth Factor (CTGF) signaling.
source: WIF1 can also antagonize Connective Tissue Growth Factor (CTGF) signaling (Surmann-Schmitt et al., 2012), which plays a supportive role in cardiac fibrosis (Travers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Surmann-Schmitt et al., 2012 and Travers et al., 2016.

claim: Wif1 was almost uniquely expressed in F-WntX in all conditions.
source: Wif1 was almost uniquely expressed in F-WntX in all conditions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes the specific expression of Wif1 in F-WntX, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: F-WntX showed upregulated multiple WNT pathway-related genes encoding WNT ligands (WNT5a, WNT16), soluble WNT antagonists (DKK3, SFRP2), membrane-bound WNT receptor (FRZB) and AXIN2.
source: Multiple other WNT pathway-related genes were upregulated in F-WntX encoding WNT ligands (WNT5a, WNT16), soluble WNT antagonists (DKK3, SFRP2), membrane-bound WNT receptor (FRZB) and AXIN2, a component of the β-catenin destruction complex (see schematic in Figure 5A; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the WNT pathway gene signature of F-WntX, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: F-WntX also showed upregulated Fmod, which inhibits fibrillogenesis and sequesters pro-fibrotic factor TGF-β within ECM.
source: F-WntX also showed upregulated Fmod, which inhibits fibrillogenesis and sequesters pro-fibrotic factor TGF-β within ECM (Zheng et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2017b) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2014 and Zheng et al., 2017b.

claim: The gene signature of F-WntX suggests an anti-WNT, anti-CTGF and anti-TGF-β extracellular and intracellular signaling milieu for F-WntX cells.
source: Overall, this signature suggests an anti-WNT, anti-CTGF and anti-TGF-β extracellular and intracellular signaling milieu for F-WntX cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression signature of F-WntX.

claim: F-WntX cells expressed Postn(Periostin), Acta2(αSMA), Tagln(Transgelin) and Scx(Scleraxis), in both sham and MI conditions, suggesting an activated state even in the absence of injury.
source: F-WntX cells expressed Postn(Periostin), Acta2(αSMA), Tagln(Transgelin) and Scx(Scleraxis), in both sham and MI conditions (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting an activated state even in the absence of injury (Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017).
evidence: This describes the activation marker expression in F-WntX, supported by Figure 5B and citation.

claim: F-Trans did not express activation markers, nor the WNT signature identified in F-WntX, or other uniquely identifying markers.
source: The adjacent cluster, F-Trans, did not express activation markers, nor the WNT signature identified in F-WntX, or other uniquely identifying markers; however, cell trajectory analysis, described below, allowed us to assign F-Trans as a transitionary population between F-WntX and F-SL fibroblasts.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of F-Trans based on gene expression and trajectory analysis.

claim: Cell trajectory analysis allowed assignment of F-Trans as a transitionary population between F-WntX and F-SL fibroblasts.
source: The adjacent cluster, F-Trans, did not express activation markers, nor the WNT signature identified in F-WntX, or other uniquely identifying markers; however, cell trajectory analysis, described below, allowed us to assign F-Trans as a transitionary population between F-WntX and F-SL fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from trajectory analysis.

claim: The top GO BP term in F-WntX was regulation of cell proliferation; however, F-WntX did not express cell cycle markers under any condition.
source: The top GO BP term in F-WntX was regulation of cell proliferation (Figure 5C); however, F-WntX did not express cell cycle markers under any condition.
evidence: This describes a GO term result and observation about cell cycle marker expression, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Analysis of Molecular Function (MF) terms in F-WntX revealed over-representation of signaling receptor binding and growth factor binding.
source: Analysis of Molecular Function (MF) terms revealed over-representation of signaling receptor binding and growth factor binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), overlapping significantly with regulation of cell proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D; Fisher's exact test, p<1e-03).
evidence: This is a result from GO MF analysis, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the regulation of cell proliferation term in F-WntX, there were several cytokine and chemokine genes, including Pdgfa, Tgfb3, Ptn, Ccl19 and Cxcl12, some of which bind receptors that were down-regulated in F-WntX, strongly suggesting paracrine functions.
source: In this latter term, there were several cytokine and chemokine genes, including Pdgfa, Tgfb3, Ptn, Ccl19 and Cxcl12, some of which bind receptors that were down-regulated in F-WntX, strongly suggesting paracrine functions related to their expression in F-WntX (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression pattern suggesting paracrine function, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Ligand-receptor analysis indicated that F-WntX cells communicate most significantly with ECs.
source: A paracrine function for F-WntX was supported by our ligand-receptor analysis, which indicated that F-WntX cells communicate most significantly with ECs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the ligand-receptor network analysis, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Analysis of top upregulated ligands in F-WntX connecting to receptors in ECs identified several factors such as Ptn(pleiotrophin), Myoc(myocilin) and Timp3(TIMP metallopeptidase inhibitor 3).
source: Analysis of top upregulated ligands in F-WntX connecting to receptors in ECs (Figure 5D) identified several factors such as Ptn(pleiotrophin), Myoc(myocilin) and Timp3(TIMP metallopeptidase inhibitor 3).
evidence: This is a result from the ligand-receptor network analysis, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: For ligands expressed in F-WntX connecting to ECs, the corresponding receptor was expressed in ECs but downregulated in F-WntX.
source: Here again, the corresponding receptor was expressed in ECs but downregulated in F-WntX (Figure 5E).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of ligand-receptor pairs, supported by Figure 5E.

claim: WIF1 protein was detected only in the infarct border zone at MI-day 3, but not in sham hearts or at MI-days 1 or 7.
source: Interestingly, we detected WIF1 protein only in the infarct border zone at MI-day 3, but not in sham hearts or at MI-days 1 or 7 (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by Figure 6.

claim: In cardiac cells, WIF1 staining was perinuclear, and co-expression of WIF1 and the golgi marker GM130 was demonstrated.
source: In cardiac cells (and some embryonic cells) WIF1 staining was perinuclear, and we demonstrated co-expression of WIF1 and the golgi marker GM130 (Figure 6D), consistent with WIF1 being a secreted protein.
evidence: This is a result from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by Figure 6D.

claim: WIF1 was found in ~4% of total nuclei of the infarct border zone at MI-day 3, with a fraction of these (~5%) being GFP+ by IF, indicating a fibroblast identity.
source: We found WIF1 in ~4% of total nuclei of the infarct border zone at MI-day 3, with a fraction of these (~5%) being GFP+ by IF, indicating a fibroblast identity (Figure 6C,I), and overall ~17% were positive for Ki67 (Figure 6E,I).
evidence: This is a result from quantification of immunofluorescence images, supported by Figure 6.

claim: Overall ~17% of WIF1+ cells were positive for Ki67.
source: We found WIF1 in ~4% of total nuclei of the infarct border zone at MI-day 3, with a fraction of these (~5%) being GFP+ by IF, indicating a fibroblast identity (Figure 6C,I), and overall ~17% were positive for Ki67 (Figure 6E,I).
evidence: This is a result from quantification of immunofluorescence images, supported by Figure 6.

claim: WIF1+ cells were negative for CD31, and negative or very low for αSMA, with rare exceptions.
source: WIF1+ cells were negative for CD31, and negative or very low for αSMA, with rare exceptions (Figure 6F,F',H).
evidence: This is a result from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by Figure 6.

claim: WIF1 was expressed in ~4% of total CD45+ cells in the infarct border zone (~15% of WIF1+ cells were CD45+).
source: However, WIF1 was also expressed in ~4% of total CD45+ cells in the infarct border zone (~15% of WIF1+ cells were CD45+) (Figure 6G,I).
evidence: This is a result from quantification of immunofluorescence images, supported by Figure 6.

claim: Frequent close proximity or contact between WIF1+ cells and CD31+ ECs was observed in tissue sections.
source: We observed frequent close proximity or contact between WIF1+ cells and CD31+ ECs in tissue sections (Figure 6H), in line with the predicted cell-cell ligand-receptor connection between F-WntX cells and ECs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from immunofluorescence analysis, supported by Figure 6H.

claim: WIF1 expression is post-transcriptionally regulated and injury-dependent, appearing in the infarct border-zone at MI-day 3 in a subset of fibroblasts and immune cells.
source: Overall, our data suggest that WIF1 expression is post-transcriptionally regulated and injury-dependent, appearing in the infarct border-zone at MI-day 3 in a subset of fibroblasts and immune cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence and scRNA-seq data.

claim: The temporal window of WIF1 expression overlaps with fibroblast activation and expansion, and the beginning of EC renewal and MYO differentiation.
source: The temporal window of WIF1 expression overlaps with fibroblast activation and expansion, and the beginning of EC renewal and MYO differentiation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics of WIF1 expression in relation to other cellular processes.

claim: MI-day 7 was characterized by the appearance of a large population of myofibroblasts (MYO), representing 52% of GFP+ cells at MI-day 7.
source: MI-day 7 was characterized by the appearance of a large population of myofibroblasts (MYO), representing 52% of GFP+ cells at MI-day 7 in our data (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This describes the proportion of MYO at MI-day 7, supported by Figure 4.

claim: MYO showed strong upregulation of numerous collagen genes (e.g. Col1a1, Col3a1, Col5a2), as well as Postn (99.5%) and Acta2 (61%) at high levels.
source: MYO showed strong upregulation of numerous collagen genes (e.g. Col1a1, Col3a1, Col5a2), as well as Postn (99.5%) and Acta2 (61%) at high levels, indicative of an activated state and suggestive of a contractile phenotype for a subset of cells (Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017; Travers et al., 2016) (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the gene expression signature of MYO, supported by Figure 4E and citations.

claim: Upregulated genes in MYO involved in wound healing and cell migration included Fn(Fibronectin) and Cthrc1(Collagen Triple Helix Repeat Containing I), the latter representing a highly specific marker for MYO.
source: Upregulated genes involved in wound healing and cell migration included Fn(Fibronectin) and Cthrc1(Collagen Triple Helix Repeat Containing I), the latter representing a highly specific marker for MYO (Figure 4F).
evidence: This describes specific marker genes for MYO, supported by Figure 4F.

claim: MYO showed decreased expression of Pdgfra, Pdgfra-GFP, Ly6a(Sca1), Thy1(Cd90) and Cd34, indicating loss of stem/progenitor cell markers.
source: MYO showed decreased expression of Pdgfra, Pdgfra-GFP, Ly6a(Sca1), Thy1(Cd90) and Cd34 (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 4), indicating loss of stem/progenitor cell markers.
evidence: This describes the downregulation of stem/progenitor markers in MYO, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: A distinct increase in a population with a signature consistent with activated fibroblasts (Fibroblast: activated; F-Act) was observed earlier in the injury process.
source: Earlier in the injury process, there was a distinct increase in a population with a signature consistent with activated fibroblasts (Fibroblast: activated; F-Act).
evidence: This describes the temporal appearance of F-Act.

claim: F-Act represented 48% of GFP+ cells at MI-day 3, before diminishing to 12% at MI-day 7.
source: These represented 48% of GFP+ cells at MI-day 3, before diminishing to 12% at MI-day 7 (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of F-Act, supported by Figure 4.

claim: F-Act expressed Postn at high levels in ~80% of cells consistent with an activated state.
source: F-Act expressed Postn at high levels in ~80% of cells (Figure 4E) consistent with an activated state (Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017).
evidence: This describes Postn expression in F-Act, supported by Figure 4E and citation.

claim: F-Act expressed Acta2 in 28% and 35% of cells at MI-day 3 and MI-day 7, respectively, although at much lower levels compared to MYO.
source: They expressed Acta2 in 28% and 35% of cells at MI-day 3 and MI-day 7, respectively, although at much lower levels compared to MYO, suggesting an emerging contractile phenotype in some cells.
evidence: This describes Acta2 expression in F-Act compared to MYO.

claim: On the population dendrogram, F-Act was most closely related to fibroblast populations (F-SH, F-SL, F-Trans) and was more distant from MYO.
source: On the population dendrogram, F-Act was most closely related to fibroblast populations (F-SH, F-SL, F-Trans) and was more distant from MYO (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from hierarchical clustering analysis, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: The top upregulated gene in F-Act was Cilp, encoding a matricellular protein and inhibitor of TGF-β1 signaling.
source: Whereas F-Act expressed few genes that could be considered highly specific, the top upregulated gene was Cilp (Figure 4F), encoding a matricellular protein and inhibitor of TGF-β1 signaling, consistent with F-Act being a pre-MYO population in which fibrosis is constrained.
evidence: This describes the top marker gene for F-Act, supported by Figure 4F.

claim: The expansion of F-Act at MI-day 3 correlated with a decrease in the proportion of F-SH and F-SL.
source: The expansion of F-Act at MI-day 3 correlated with a decrease in the proportion of F-SH and F-SL, whereas the diminishment of the F-Act population at MI-day 7 coincided with the appearance of MYO and an apparent partial restoration of F-SH and F-SL cells (Figure 1A,E; Figure 4A,D; see Discussion).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics and correlations between fibroblast populations, supported by Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The diminishment of the F-Act population at MI-day 7 coincided with the appearance of MYO and an apparent partial restoration of F-SH and F-SL cells.
source: The expansion of F-Act at MI-day 3 correlated with a decrease in the proportion of F-SH and F-SL, whereas the diminishment of the F-Act population at MI-day 7 coincided with the appearance of MYO and an apparent partial restoration of F-SH and F-SL cells (Figure 1A,E; Figure 4A,D; see Discussion).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics and correlations between fibroblast populations, supported by Figures 1 and 4.

claim: A distinct GFP+ population contained fibroblasts undergoing proliferation (Fibroblast - cycling; F-Cyc), comprising 15% of GFP+ cells at MI-day 3 and 3% at MI-day 7.
source: A distinct GFP+ population contained fibroblasts undergoing proliferation (Fibroblast - cycling; F-Cyc), comprising 15% of GFP+ cells at MI-day 3 and 3% at MI-day 7 (Figure 4D), consistent with studies showing peak fibroblast proliferation at MI-days 2–4 (Fu et al., 2018; Ivey et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the proportion of F-Cyc at different time points, supported by Figure 4D and citations.

claim: F-Cyc uniquely expressed a strong cell cycle gene signature, including Ccnb2(CyclinB), Cdk1(Cyclin dependent kinase 1) and Mki67(Ki67).
source: F-Cyc uniquely expressed a strong cell cycle gene signature, including Ccnb2(CyclinB), Cdk1(Cyclin dependent kinase 1) and Mki67(Ki67) (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3), and expressed both Postn (88%) and Acta2 (76%) at high levels (Figure 4E; see below).
evidence: This describes the gene expression signature of F-Cyc, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: F-Cyc expressed both Postn (88%) and Acta2 (76%) at high levels.
source: F-Cyc uniquely expressed a strong cell cycle gene signature, including Ccnb2(CyclinB), Cdk1(Cyclin dependent kinase 1) and Mki67(Ki67) (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3), and expressed both Postn (88%) and Acta2 (76%) at high levels (Figure 4E; see below).
evidence: This describes activation marker expression in F-Cyc, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Diffusion Map analysis showed MYO, F-WntX and F-Cyc were represented as three different trajectories along diffusion components 1, 2 and 3, respectively, with the root containing F-SH and F-SL.
source: To look at potential relationships between the major GFP+ populations, we analyzed cell trajectories using Diffusion Maps (Materials and methods). MYO, F-WntX and F-Cyc were represented as three different trajectories along diffusion components 1, 2 and 3, respectively (Figure 7A), with the root containing the two large unactivated fibroblast populations F-SH and F-SL, which were most prominent in sham hearts.
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map trajectory analysis, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: F-Trans was an intermediary population along the trajectory to F-WntX.
source: F-Trans was an intermediary population along the trajectory to F-WntX, and F-Act was an intermediary population for both F-Cyc and MYO branches.
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map trajectory analysis.

claim: F-Act was an intermediary population for both F-Cyc and MYO branches.
source: F-Trans was an intermediary population along the trajectory to F-WntX, and F-Act was an intermediary population for both F-Cyc and MYO branches.
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map trajectory analysis.

claim: F-Cyc was represented most strongly at MI-day 3, whereas MYO was exclusively associated with MI-day 7.
source: F-Cyc, characterized by expression of a strong cell cycle gene signature, was represented most strongly at MI-day 3, whereas MYO was exclusively associated with MI-day 7 (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This describes the temporal distribution of F-Cyc and MYO, supported by Figure 7B,C.

claim: The data suggest that F-Act expands by proliferation up to MI-day 3 (F-Cyc trajectory) and differentiates to MYO during the transition from MI-day 3 to MI-day 7.
source: These data suggest that F-Act expands by proliferation up to MI-day 3 (F-Cyc trajectory) and differentiates to MYO during the transition from MI-day 3 to MI-day 7.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trajectory analysis and temporal dynamics.

claim: The presence of some F-Cyc-like cells between the F-Cyc and MYO trajectories at MI-day 7 raises the possibility that a small fraction of F-Act cells differentiate rapidly into MYO after or during division.
source: The presence of some F-Cyc-like cells between the F-Cyc and MYO trajectories at MI-day 7 raises the possibility that a small fraction of F-Act cells differentiate rapidly into MYO after or during division (see below).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the trajectory analysis.

claim: DE genes for F-Act were over-represented in terms for collagen fibril organization and regulation of wound healing.
source: DE genes for F-Act were over-represented in terms for collagen fibril organization (including several collagen genes) and regulation of wound healing.
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of differentially expressed genes in F-Act.

claim: There was an additional large gene signature strongly upregulated in MYO compared to F-Act.
source: Many of these genes were also expressed in F-Cyc and MYO; however, there was an additional large gene signature strongly upregulated in MYO compared to F-Act (Figure 7D).
evidence: This describes differential gene expression between MYO and F-Act, supported by Figure 7D.

claim: DE genes for MYO demonstrated GO BP terms for collagen fibril organization and cell adhesion.
source: DE genes for MYO demonstrated GO BP terms for collagen fibril organization and cell adhesion, containing collagen genes Col3a1, Col5a1, Col11a1 and Col14a1, and others involved in cell:cell and cell:matrix adhesion including Thbs1 (encoding Thrombospondin 1) and Fbn1.
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of differentially expressed genes in MYO.

claim: Other GO BP terms for MYO included angiogenesis and heart development as well as negative regulation of canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Other terms included angiogenesis and heart development as well as negative regulation of canonical Wnt signaling pathway, containing many genes previously identified in F-WntX.
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of differentially expressed genes in MYO.

claim: Minor GFP+ populations included epicardial cells (EPI), observed only at MI-day 7.
source: Minor GFP+ populations included epicardial cells (EPI), observed only at MI-day 7.
evidence: This describes a minor population identified in the GFP+ dataset.

claim: EPI expressed Wt1 and overall were related transcriptionally to dissected adult mouse epicardium (Spearman's correlation test, p=0.014, r = 0.26).
source: These expressed Wt1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and overall were related transcriptionally to dissected adult mouse epicardium (Bochmann et al., 2010) (Spearman's correlation test, p=0.014, r = 0.26).
evidence: This describes the marker expression and transcriptional similarity of EPI, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citation.

claim: EPI are likely to be epicardial-derived fibroblasts that arise after MI as the epicardium reactivates its developmental program (including Pdgfra expression).
source: These are likely to be epicardial-derived fibroblasts that arise after MI as the epicardium reactivates its developmental program (including Pdgfra expression) (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EPI population identity, supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Epicardial cells were not detected in TIP data, suggesting that these cells are under-sampled in the experiments.
source: Consistent with a previous cardiac scRNA-seq analysis on uninjured hearts (Skelly et al., 2018), we did not detect epicardial cells in TIP data, suggesting that these cells are under-sampled in our experiments - this is likely technical as epicardial cells have been detected readily in single-nucleus RNA-seq (Hu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation about the absence of epicardial cells in TIP, with citations to previous studies.

claim: The minor population F-IFNS was found in all conditions, was negative for Cd45 and expressed high levels of Col1a1 and other fibroblast markers, demonstrating a fibroblast identity.
source: The minor population F-IFNS (Fibroblast: Interferon stimulated), found in all conditions, was negative for Cd45 and expressed high levels of Col1a1 and other fibroblast markers (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3), demonstrating a fibroblast identity, and interferon-responsive genes (Figure 4F; Supplementary file 4) (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of F-IFNS, supported by Figure 4E and citation.

claim: F-IFNS expressed interferon-responsive genes.
source: The minor population F-IFNS (Fibroblast: Interferon stimulated), found in all conditions, was negative for Cd45 and expressed high levels of Col1a1 and other fibroblast markers (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3), demonstrating a fibroblast identity, and interferon-responsive genes (Figure 4F; Supplementary file 4) (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the gene expression signature of F-IFNS, supported by Figure 4F and citation.

claim: Scleraxis was expressed in F-WntX cells and MYO.
source: Several TF genes expressed in GFP+ cells may drive differentiation or responses to environmental stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 4). Scleraxis, already mentioned, was expressed in F-WntX cells and MYO.
evidence: This describes the expression of Scleraxis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tcf21, an accepted marker of cardiac fibroblasts, was expressed in most GFP+ populations with the exception of F-WntX cells.
source: The basic helix-loop-helix factor gene, Tcf21, an accepted marker of cardiac fibroblasts (Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017), was expressed in most GFP+ populations with the exception of F-WntX cells.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of Tcf21, with citation to Tallquist and Molkentin, 2017.

claim: Tbx20 was expressed across all GFP+ cells and upregulated in F-WntX.
source: T-box factor gene Tbx20, another fibroblast marker, was expressed across all GFP+ cells and upregulated in F-WntX.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of Tbx20.

claim: Meox1, which is part of the cardiac fetal gene expression signature reactivated in injured hearts, showed upregulation in subsets of GFP+ cells, most prominently in activated populations (F-Act, F-Wntx, F-Cyc and MYO).
source: The homeodomain TF gene, Meox1, which is part of the cardiac fetal gene expression signature reactivated in injured hearts (Lu et al., 2018), showed upregulation in subsets of GFP+ cells, most prominently in activated populations (F-Act, F-Wntx, F-Cyc and MYO), and may drive the activated state.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of Meox1, with citation to Lu et al., 2018.

claim: Prrx1 was expressed across all GFP+ populations in all conditions.
source: Interestingly, the homeodomain TF gene, Prrx1, which in BM is expressed in a subset of mesenchymal cells with CFU-F and multi-lineage differentiation potential (Kfoury and Scadden, 2015), was expressed across all GFP+ populations in all conditions.
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of Prrx1, with citation to Kfoury and Scadden, 2015.

claim: Re-clustering of the GFP+ day 3 dataset revealed that F-Cyc could be sub-divided into two populations, with only one exhibiting a clear cell cycle signature.
source: We re-clustered the sham and MI datasets at days 3 and 7 individually (Figure 8A,B), and repeated Diffusion Map analysis of GFP+ fibroblast lineages (Figure 8C,D) (Materials and methods). Whereas most populations identified at day 3 directly corresponded to those identified in the aggregate analysis, we found that F-Cyc could now be sub-divided into two populations, with only one exhibiting a clear cell cycle signature (Figure 8E, Supplementary file 7; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is a result from re-clustering analysis of the GFP+ day 3 dataset, supported by Figure 8.

claim: An intermediary population (Fibroblast - Cycling Intermediate; F-CI) showed upregulation of fibroblast activation markers including Postn, Cthrc1 and Acta2, but did not express markers of cell cycle.
source: An intermediary population (Fibroblast - Cycling Intermediate; F-CI) showed upregulation of fibroblast activation markers including Postn, Cthrc1 and Acta2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), but did not express markers of cell cycle, suggesting that it represents an additional population of activated fibroblasts, potentially competent for cell cycle entry.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of F-CI, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: F-CI also upregulated genes involved in protein translation, a signature absent in F-Act.
source: F-CI also upregulated genes involved in protein translation, a signature absent in F-Act (Figure 8E).
evidence: This describes a unique gene signature of F-CI, supported by Figure 8E.

claim: Based on an iRF classifier, no corresponding F-CI cluster was found at MI-day 7, indicating its transient nature.
source: Based on an iRF classifier trained to predict MI-day 3 populations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), we found no corresponding F-CI cluster at MI-day 7, indicating its transient nature (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is a result from the iRF classifier prediction, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diffusion Map analysis lent weight to the hypothesis that F-CI is a transitory population between F-Act and F-Cyc at MI-Day 3.
source: Diffusion Map analysis also lent weight to the hypothesis that F-CI is a transitory population between F-Act and F-Cyc at MI-Day 3 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map trajectory analysis, supported by Figure 8C.

claim: After removing cell cycle genes at MI-day 3, 88% of F-Cyc cells merged with F-CI, strongly supporting the hypothesis that F-CI is a pre-proliferative precursor of F-Cyc.
source: We next removed genes annotated with the GO term 'Cell Cycle' and re-clustered populations. At MI-day 3, 88% of F-Cyc cells merged with F-CI, strongly supporting the hypothesis that F-CI is a pre-proliferative precursor of F-Cyc (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a result from re-clustering after removing cell cycle genes, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: After removal of cell cycle genes at MI-day 7, 65% of F-Cyc cells remained as a distinct (proliferative) population, although 26% merged with F-Act and 6% merged with the MYO populations.
source: After removal of cell cycle genes at MI-day 7, 65% of F-Cyc cells remained as a distinct (proliferative) population, although 26% merged with F-Act and 6% merged with the MYO populations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a result from re-clustering after removing cell cycle genes, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The data indicate that the closest population to the majority F-CI and cycling cells is F-Act rather than MYO.
source: Taken together with Diffusion Map analysis, these data indicate that the closest population to the majority F-CI and cycling cells is F-Act rather than MYO, even though both express Acta2 and other MYO markers at high levels (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the re-clustering and trajectory analysis.

claim: A minority of F-Cyc cells at MI-day 7 may be dividing MYO cells or in transition to MYO.
source: However, a minority of F-Cyc cells at MI-day 7 may be dividing MYO cells or in transition to MYO (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the re-clustering analysis.

claim: The data support the idea that F-CI cells are an activated form of fibroblast closely related to F-Cyc and derivative of F-Act.
source: Our data support the idea that F-CI cells are an activated form of fibroblast closely related to F-Cyc and derivative of F-Act.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clustering and trajectory analysis.

claim: In the MI-day 7 re-analysis, MYO could be sub-divided into three clusters - MYO-1, MYO-2 and MYO-3.
source: In the MI-day 7 re-analysis, we found that MYO could be sub-divided into three clusters - MYO-1, MYO-2 and MYO-3 (Figure 8B,F; Supplementary file 9; Supplementary file 10), and comparing these clusters we noted genes corresponding to the contrasting functions of fibrosis inhibition and promotion.
evidence: This is a result from re-clustering analysis of the GFP+ day 7 dataset, supported by Figure 8B,F.

claim: MYO-2 upregulated Tgfb1 (encoding TGF-β1), Scx(Scleraxis), and Thbs4(Thrombospondin 4).
source: MYO-2 upregulated Tgfb1 (encoding TGF-β1), which is one of the strongest and most studied drivers of MYO formation (Figure 8G; Supplementary file 9), Scx(Scleraxis), which regulates ECM production and the myofibroblast phenotype downstream of TGF-β (Bagchi et al., 2016) and Thbs4(Thrombospondin 4), a regulator of cardiac fibrosis (Frolova et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the gene expression signature of MYO-2, supported by Figure 8G and citations.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation with TGF-β treatment in DE genes comparing MYO-2 v MYO-1 (Spearman's correlation test, r = 0.26, Padj = 1.93e-12) and MYO-3 v MYO-1 (Spearman's correlation test, r = 0.25, Padj = 1.75e-10).
source: For inter-MYO comparisons, we found a significant positive correlation with TGF-β treatment in DE genes comparing MYO-2 v MYO-1 (Spearman's correlation test, r = 0.26, Padj = 1.93e-12) and MYO-3 v MYO-1 (Spearman's correlation test, r = 0.25, Padj = 1.75e-10), supporting the conclusion that MYO-2 and MYO-3 are pro-fibrotic.
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis with TGF-β treatment data.

claim: MYO-1 showed strong upregulation of anti-fibrosis genes included Wisp2, encoding matricellular protein CCN5 which can reverse established fibrosis, and Sfrp2 encoding a soluble WNT receptor and antagonist of canonical WNT signalling, which is pro-fibrotic.
source: In contrast, MYO-1 showed strong upregulation of anti-fibrosis genes included Wisp2, encoding matricellular protein CCN5 which can reverse established fibrosis (Jeong et al., 2016), and Sfrp2 encoding a soluble WNT receptor and antagonist of canonical WNT signalling, which is pro-fibrotic (Mirotsou et al., 2007) (Figure 8G).
evidence: This describes the gene expression signature of MYO-1, supported by Figure 8G and citations.

claim: MYO-1 upregulated genes showed significant GO terms negative regulation of growth factor stimulus and negative regulation of cell proliferation.
source: MYO-1 upregulated genes showed significant GO terms negative regulation of growth factor stimulus and negative regulation of cell proliferation (Figure 8F; Supplementary file 10), which included Sfrp1, implicated in inhibition of fibroblast proliferation and fibrosis (Sklepkiewicz et al., 2015), and Htra1 and Htra3, implicated in TGF-β signaling inhibition (Tocharus et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of MYO-1 upregulated genes, supported by Figure 8F and citations.

claim: Diffusion Map analysis of MYO sub-populations showed that MYO-1 and MYO-2 were distinct clusters with some overlap, suggesting a continuum of states, whereas MYO-3 did not appear to be a distinct population.
source: Diffusion Map analysis of MYO sub-populations showed that MYO-1 and MYO-2 were distinct clusters with some overlap, suggesting a continuum of states, whereas MYO-3 did not appear to be a distinct population (Figure 8—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a result from Diffusion Map analysis of MYO sub-populations, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1G.
